transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2025-08-21 14:00 PDT
Duration: 45 mins
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam Park (Redwood SE), Sara Nguyen (BlueHorizon CTO), Devon Patel (Product), Riley Torres (ML Engineer)

Summary: quick demo of JSON/structured-output mode, example function calling for downstream service enforcement, and Console/Optimize hooks to tune batching and quantization. Some stumbles on transcription of product names.

[00:00] Maya: hey everyone thanks for making time, we'll walk through our structured output and function calling flow and then show Console + Optimize suggestions. uh Liam will drive the demo.
[00:22] Liam: cool, hi all. so first thing, JSON mode — this is where you define a schema for the output, you can mark fields required, types, arrays, nested-ish but we try to keep the shape stable. for BH use-case you mentioned product metadata + pricing predictions so we built an example schema.
[00:45] Riley: can you show how you prevent hallucinations where model invents an id or a vendor name?
[00:52] Liam: yeah good q. two levers: schema validation (we run a strict parser on the response and reject nonconforming outputs), and function-calling where we map structured outputs to a typed call to an internal microservice so you never persist free text. also we have optional guardrails — confidence thresholds and rerank/fallback policies.
[01:20] Devon: when you say function-calling is that the same as openai function-calling? will it call our service?
[01:28] Maya: similar idea — you define the function signatures in the Console or via API, include param types (strings, numbers, enums), and the runtime will either return the JSON or call the webhook. we support both hosted and dedicated routing; for private VPC you can webhook into your internal endpoint.
[01:48] Sara: okay what about schema evolution? our product model changes quarterly.
[01:55] Liam: we support versioned schemas. you can pin a model+schema pair in the route, and Console keeps schema diffs; rollouts can be canaryed across traffic. if a new schema rejects too many responses, we surface a regression alert in Optimize and you can auto-fallback.
[02:18] Riley: show us an example — like, a sample response and a failed parse.
[02:23] Liam: sure, demo screen sharing... (typing) here's a sample prompt: "Extract product record, price, manufacturer, SKU, confidence". Model returns JSON, we run a strict parse and then we do a post-parse check; if the SKU doesn't match format we mark it invalid and either ask for regeneration or map to a human review queue.
[02:48] Maya: i'll pull up the Console route config — this route enforces schema v1.2, has a function-calling webhook to /internal/catalog/ingest, and a fallback to lightweight hosted model if dedicated pool is saturated.
[03:10] Sara: dedicated pool — we were thinking dedicated for PII isolation, is that necessary?
[03:16] Maya: not strictly, hosted can be configured with retention controls, but Dedicated gives you reserved capacity and better isolation guarantees (and is often easier to meet enterprise SLAs). For regulated customers we recommend Private (VPC) with customer-managed KMS.
[03:35] Devon: what about latency — function calls add round trips?
[03:39] Liam: we minimize extra latency by optionally returning the structured JSON inline and then async-ing the call to your webhook, or you can choose synchronous call if you need immediate downstream execution. Optimize suggests batching and possible quantization profiles to trade cost vs latency.
[04:02] Riley: metrics — can we see per-token cost and per-route latency?
[04:07] Maya: yes Console shows token breakdown by model and route, and tracing for individual requests. We can also export traces to your telemetry.
[04:19] Devon: can we configure guardrails like only allow certain enum values for manufacturer?
[04:24] Liam: yes you can enforce enums in the JSON schema and we will reject otherwise; also you can attach a custom validation hook.
[04:36] Sara: what about SSO, audit logs, and SOC2?
[04:40] Maya: SOC 2 Type II, SSO via SAML/Okta, RBAC in Console, and audit logs that include request/response metadata (we can mask PII). we'll send the security pack after this call.
[04:55] Riley: one more technical — KV cache and long-context performance for multi-turn extraction, do you support caching intermediate keys across calls?
[05:04] Liam: yes — our serving runtime manages KV cache; for conversation you can pin cache across calls and we do chunking for long contexts. for structured extraction you often don't need huge context, but if you do, we have memory-efficient attention paths and quantized kernels.
[05:25] Maya: demo time — Liam will show the JSON mode in action and the function-calling log.
[05:32] Liam: ok screen — here's the Console UI, the route 'bh-product-extract', Schema tab shows the JSON schema, example request and expected response. I will send a prompt and you can see the parsed object.
[06:00] (short pause, typing noises)
[06:13] Liam: here's model output — looks like: {"product_name": "SolarWrap 3", "price": 129.99, "manufacturer": "SunForge", "sku": "SF-9876"}
[06:30] Riley: if model returns "sun forge" lowercased will it normalize?
[06:34] Liam: normalization rules are supported as post-processors — you can map to canonical enums or run a fuzzy match against your catalog. we also have a confidence score field.
[06:47] Devon: show function call log.
[06:49] Liam: here — function call succeeded, webhook 200 OK, response acked. you can inspect payload and raw model token output in trace. sometimes transcription shows weird labels — the model tokenization debug is available.
[07:05] Sara: any limits on nested objects in schema? we have nested spec for variants and dimensions.
[07:10] Liam: small nested structures are fine; we recommend flattening deeply nested user-facing records. there's a size/cost tradeoff. Optimize will flag large responses that increase token costs and suggest compression or field pruning.
[07:28] Maya: question for you Sara — what's success for a pilot?
[07:33] Sara: accurate extraction at 95% on our test set, sub-300ms P95 latency for inline JSON, and secure webhook inside our VPC.
[07:44] Maya: great, we can scope a 2-week pilot to validate that.
[07:48] Riley: how do we run regression tests across model upgrades?
[07:52] Liam: we have per-prompt eval sets in Console — you can pin tests that run on every rollout; quality regressions trigger alerts and we keep diffs. we also recommend canarying new model versions.
[08:05] Devon: about cost — can Optimize simulate cost per 1M requests given batching configs?
[08:11] Liam: yes Optimize has a cost simulator: you input QPS, request length, and it suggests batching, cache TTLs, quantization profile, and shows estimated token and GPU costs.
[08:22] Maya: i want to call out guardrails: for function-calling we provide strict typing, but for extra safety you can do a final validation lambda in your infra that rejects suspicious calls — our runtime supports easy retries to human review.
[08:41] Sara: legal needs to see data retention controls and where logs live.
[08:46] Maya: noted, we'll include retention options and export controls in the security pack.
[08:52] (brief cross-talk)
[09:00] Liam: quick note — sometimes the auto-transcript will mangle product names (we see SunForge vs SunnyForge) so keep an eye on canonicalization.
[09:10] Devon: is there sample code for function-calling from our backend?
[09:13] Maya: yes we'll include SDK snippets in the follow-up, Node/Python examples for both synchronous and async webhook flows.
[09:20] Riley: if we run pilot on Dedicated, how long to provision?
[09:24] Maya: dedicated pools typically 2-4 business days once contract is signed; for private VPC it's longer depending on networking (usually 1-2 weeks to coordinate).
[09:35] Sara: ok budget question — what's the pricing anchor?
[09:39] Maya: we'll send a pricing anchor post-call, but basic model usage is per-token; Dedicated is reserved monthly commit; Optimize can reduce unit costs with batching/quant profiles.
[09:51] Devon: anything we should be aware of for legal procurement?
[09:54] Maya: standard enterprise terms, addendum for data residency and custom SLA are possible. we can loop in our legal team.
[10:05] (demo wrap-up)
[10:10] Liam: last live demo — showing an example of a rejected response: model returned a string instead of array, Console logs show parse error, we replayed the prompt with a higher temperature constraint and the model produced schema-conformant output.
[10:31] Riley: nice, will be useful.
[10:35] Maya: recap and next steps: we'll send security pack, sample schema and function-calling manifest, pricing anchor, and schedule pilot kick-off; customer to share test set and target SLAs.
[10:50] Sara: thanks, this was helpful.
[10:52] Maya: thanks everyone, we will follow up with docs and links. bye.
notes: Demo included inline JSON return vs synchronous webhook options
Optimize cost simulator shown with batching and quantization recommendations
Console rollouts and schema diffs demonstrated
